blocks.text: **The task.** Given an unsorted array, find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers. The numbers need not be adjacent in the array. Required: O(N) time.
Sorting makes this easy — scan for consecutive neighbours. But sorting is O(N log N), and the problem demands O(N). We need something better.
A run has a **start**: a number whose predecessor is absent. If `x - 1` is not in the set, then `x` begins a run.
So put everything in a set, then only count upward from genuine starts. That single guard is what keeps the whole thing linear.
Why the nested loop stays O(N)
The `while` inside the `for` looks quadratic, and this is the part worth understanding.

The inner loop only runs for numbers that **start** a run. And each element is walked over by exactly one such run — the run it belongs to. So across the entire execution the inner loop performs at most N steps in total, not N per iteration.
Remove the `continue` guard and this genuinely becomes O(N²): every element of a long run would re-walk the rest of it.
Why a Set, not a Map
We only ask whether a number exists, never where it sat. A Set states that. It also deduplicates for free, so repeated values cannot inflate a run's length.
**Time: O(N)** — building the set is O(N), and the scan is O(N) by the argument above.
**Space: O(N)** for the set. This is the space-for-time trade buying us a better complexity class than sorting allows.
